connector: The last chapter. A story does its final work here: it hands out endings, and the endings show you who each character has become. Read with a then-and-now question in your head. Who is different from the person you met on the first page?

a.raw: caspian kissed the lions paw and said i dont think i do sir
a.fixed: Caspian kissed the Lion’s paw and said, “I don’t think I do, Sir.”
a.why: Capitals on Caspian, Lion’s, I and Sir; apostrophes in Lion’s and don’t; a comma before the quote and before Sir; the period goes inside the quotation marks.

b.raw: the mice said they would cut off their own tails if their chief must go without his
b.fixed: The Mice said they would cut off their own tails if their Chief must go without his.
b.why: Lewis capitalizes the Mice and their Chief like names of a people and a title; no comma before if at the end; a period ends it.

scholar.journal-q3: … and quote what Peter says to Lucy.

s4w30cf1.h1: separate ends in silent e. What happens before -ion?
s4w30cf1.why: Drop the e: separate + ion = separation.

s4w30cf2.h1: celebrate ends in silent e. What happens before -ion?
s4w30cf2.why: Drop the e: celebrate + ion = celebration.

s4w30cf3.h1: restore ends in silent e. What happens before -ation?
s4w30cf3.why: Drop the e: restore + ation = restoration.

s4w30cf4.h1: for·GET has its beat on the last syllable. Double or not?
s4w30cf4.why: Double the t: forget + t + able = forgettable.

vocab: An invitation to fight or compete that must be answered.
Fighting; single combat is one against one.
To say words aloud for someone else to write down.
An official who oversees a contest and keeps order.
The ceremony of crowning a king or queen.
The line of people you come from.
notes.wordParts: Review of the unit’s bases: port, tract, struct, spect, ject, script/scribe, rupt, duct/duce, form, plus press = push, tain = hold, lev = lift.
notes.grammar: Dialogue punctuation: quotation marks fence off the exact words; the comma or end mark goes inside the closing quotation mark; a tag like said Peter joins with a comma. Moving the tag changes the rhythm of a line.
notes.spelling: Cumulative review: a hard word is often two or three rules stacked up. Take it apart: se + par + ate + ion; forget + t + able.

virtue.title: Which pillar is it?
virtue.intro: In Chapter 15 the story hands out its endings. Read each moment. Tap the pillar it shows best.

items.t: Aslan asks Caspian if he feels himself sufficient to be King. Caspian says, “I — I don’t think I do, Sir. I’m only a kid.”
items.why: He tells the truth about himself, even about a crown.
items.hint: What could Caspian have said instead?

items.t: The Mice draw their swords, ready to cut off their own tails so their Chief won’t be the only one without one.
items.why: They give up something of their own for their leader.

items.t: Aslan offers the Telmarines a door to a new world. A burly soldier pushes forward first: “Well, I’ll take the offer.”
items.why: He goes first into the unknown.

items.t: Peter learns he will never come back to Narnia. Lucy asks if he can bear it. He says, “Well, I think I can.”
items.why: He accepts a hard ending without complaining.
items.hint: How does Peter take the news?

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Nell. This is the last chapter. Today’s question: who has changed the most since the first page, and what did the change cost them?
transcripts.read: Make a then-and-now list as you read. Caspian, Peter, Susan, Reepicheep. Who were they at the start, and who are they now? Slow down for the goodbyes, especially what Peter tells Lucy about coming back.
transcripts.spelling: A hard word is usually two or three easy rules stacked up. Hopeful: hope, plus ful, and the e stays because ful starts with a consonant. Take the word apart, use the rules one at a time, and put it back together.
